<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 15 Oct 2026 01:38:06 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Government seeks ‘negotiation process’ to avoid second round of public sector strikes ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/government-seeks-negotiation-process-to-avoid-second-round-of-public-sector-strikes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/15/government-seeks-negotiation-process-to-avoid-second-round-of-public-sector-strikes/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 20:23:56 +0000Efforts are under way to unblock the path to negotiations on a new public sector pay deal after public services were brought to a standstill by nationwide industrial action on Wednesday.

It is expected that contacts between Government and unions will now intensify as officials seek to find a way forward that could avoid next week’s scheduled second day of strikes.

Speaking in Brussels on Wednesday evening, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said there was “a sense of goodwill and a willingness to get a resolution on this”.

“The Government is open for negotiations and open for dialogue, we want to get into a negotiation process,” he said. “We will engage and see if we can find a basis and a process that would be satisfactory to all sides that enable negotiations to take place and avoid any action next week.”

There have been suggestions in Government about a possible preliminary process at the Workplace Relations Commission that could see a draft agenda for negotiations agreed, but officials remained tight-lipped on Wednesday night, citing the sensitivity of the issue. Union sources played down the suggestion of a fresh initiative from Government, though it is understood informal contacts are continuing.

Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan said that recent comments by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers suggested “there may be a pathway” to negotiations on a new deal.

Callinan chairs the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (Ictu), which is due to meet on Thursday to review the situation.

Some individual unions whose members participated in the strike action met on Wednesday night to take stock and consider how to proceed if no agreement is reached and next week’s strike goes ahead.

Chambers, though, told RTÉ there was “intensive work that’s going on in the background”, and “that in the next day or so we’ll be able to set out a further context”.

Public opinion may shift if the second strike goes ahead

“I’m conscious that we have to progress that in the coming hours and, indeed, in the next day or so,” he said.

He continued to strike a more conciliatory tone, saying he understood the “significant pressure” that public sector workers were under, adding, “They need a new pay deal delivered.”

He said the aim of Government was for a new agreement that is a “fair, meaningful and credible deal” for workers, but added that any deal had to be “sustainable and affordable” for the State.

He said he was “absolutely” happy for the issue of pay to be dealt with as a priority in any negotiations – a key demand of the unions – but he noted that union leaders had accepted that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed”.

Chambers praised public sector workers for doing “an incredible job” and said he hoped “we’ll find a way forward” in the “next day or so”.

Unions claimed widespread public support on the picket lines as industrial action shut schools, colleges, local and national Government offices and severely restricted health services across the country yesterday. The HSE said that appointments cancelled yesterday would be “prioritised and rescheduled as soon as possible”.

Health service workers claim no choice but to strike

However, it indicated that uncertainty about next week’s planned stoppage would impact its plans. “We ask patients to bear with us as there may be further delays until there is greater certainty regarding future industrial action,” the HSE said in a statement.

More than 150 schools in the Dublin and Kildare regions received threatening emails warning of potential attacks on Wednesday. The motive was not clear and the schools continued to operate as normal while taking advice from gardaí.

Opposition parties all declared support for the strikes and urged the Government to enter negotiations and agree pay increases for public servants.

Speaking outside a closed Leinster House, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said the Government had “played a really terrible and disrespectful game of chicken with 300,000 workers that we all rely on ... I think you can feel the really strong sense of public support for all of the workers”.

]]><![CDATA[Wall Street slips after inflation shock as ASML lifts European tech]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/wall-street-slips-after-inflation-shock-as-asml-lifts-european-tech/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/wall-street-slips-after-inflation-shock-as-asml-lifts-european-tech/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 17:30:03 +0000Battered by weeks of elevated oil prices and government bond yields, European investors had pinned their hopes ⁠on corporate earnings to breathe life into equities, but results have been uneven so far.

Now, on Wednesday, hotter-than-expected inflation readings in the US have revived fears of higher interest rates.

The news sent Wall Street lower following a rally in shares among European technology firms earlier in the day, led by chipmaking equipment group ASML.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index fell by 0.9 per cent to close at 14,084.62 on Wednesday afternoon.

Kerry Group continued its advance, with shares up 0.8 per cent to €91.30. Since the beginning of the week, its shares have risen more than 4 per cent.

The next biggest riser in the day was property developer Glenveagh, which saw its price up 0.6 per cent to €2.35, followed by Glanbia, which was up 0.6 per cent to €20.10.

Larger losses were recorded by companies at the other end of the index, with shares in Ryanair down by almost 2.7 per cent to €22.10.

Gene Murtagh’s Kingspan group saw its share price fall by close to 1.5 per cent to €101.50, while Mincon Group slipped 1 per cent to €0.99.

London

The FTSE 100 ended up 0.7 per cent at 10,724.86 on Wednesday, lifted by consumer and defence stocks.

Among consumer staple firms to rise were Unilever and Burberry, which gained 2.5 per cent and 3 per cent respectively. British American Tobacco was up 0.7 per cent, while spirits maker Diageo was up 1 per cent.

Elsewhere, following a call from activist investor Ancora for a strategic review, the self-storage firm Big Yellow rose 5.4 per cent.

Financial services firm Admiral slipped 2.6 per cent after Peel Hunt ‌cut its price target, warning ⁠the insurer’s UK motor policy growth could slow as it raises rates to protect margins.

Defence products maker Chemring climbed 2.4 per cent after its Roke unit secured a partnership with a major US contractor, including an ​initial $16 million order and a minimum $170 million (€152 million) agreement over five ​years.

Europe

European shares notched slim gains after robust earnings from ASML reassured investors concerned about AI demand.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index gained 0.43 per cent to 637.75 points on Wednesday. The healthcare index was the biggest gainer on the benchmark, rising 2.3 per cent to hit its highest since early September.

Shares of semiconductor firm ASML rose 1.2 per cent after it said customers were already ​looking to place orders for its advanced chipmaking tools for 2029 and 2030, illustrating that demand remains sturdy.

Among other movers, Orsted dropped 3.9 per cent following a report by Bloomberg News that the US ‌would re-evaluate the permit for its ⁠wind farm near Rhode Island.

New York

Wall Street stocks fell on ​Wednesday after data showed US consumer prices rose more than expected last month, reinforcing expectations the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates as soon as this month.

US Labour Department data showed the core consumer price index (CPI) was up 0.3 per cent in September versus economist expectations for a rise of 0.2 per cent. On ​an annual basis, core CPI, which strips out food and energy prices, rose 2.6 per cent, above forecasts for a rise of 2.5 per cent. The headline rate ⁠rose 3.7 per cent, above estimates for a rise of 3.6 per cent.

On Wall Street, all three indexes were trading lower, with technology and industrials driving losses while healthcare, consumer staples and energy stocks were higher.

In early afternoon trading, the Dow Jones was down 0.3 per cent, the S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent and the Nasdaq was 1.62 per cent lower.

Large US banks reported earnings on Wednesday, with Bank of America saying profits fell in the third quarter and Morgan Stanley showing it beat expectations for its third-quarter ‌profit thanks to strong equity ⁠trading.

The S&P 500 technology index traded at a two-week low, as chip stocks came under pressure again. They lost ground on Tuesday after reports pointing to progress in chip design by China’s CXMT fuelled competition concerns.

Shares of Intel and Micron fell 2.6 per cent and one per cent, respectively, while Nvidia slipped 1.7 per cent.

Most Magnificent Seven stocks declined, barring Alphabet and Apple, which rose 0.2 per cent and 0.9 per cent, respectively. – Additional reporting: Reuters

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Tech leaders outline AI dangers and opportunities at Dublin summit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/tech-leaders-outline-ai-dangers-and-opportunities-at-dublin-summit/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/tech-leaders-outline-ai-dangers-and-opportunities-at-dublin-summit/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 16:06:49 +0000The artificial intelligence (AI) industry needs strict guardrails and standards to ensure the technology is safe, the International AI Summit in Dublin heard on Wednesday.

Tech leaders from Microsoft, Google, Stripe and IBM gathered at the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4, alongside policymakers to discuss the opportunities and issues facing the industry.

Cofounder and chairman of Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis said recent incidents of AI agents going “rogue” and hacking third-party systems were “early warning shots”.

AI will not bring about ‘displacement’ in public service, says Taoiseach

“The systems aren’t that powerful yet, so the incidents aren’t that major, but they could be looking into next year and the next couple of years if we don’t do more work as an industry and individually as companies and governments,” he said.

“There’s a lot of work that we can bring best practices from other sectors that have dealt with safety-critical systems, whether it’s biology or nuclear. I think there’s a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems, and I think we need to start taking that seriously and bring experts in from those areas.”

Hassabis has backed the establishment of a standards body that would help develop the technology in a “nuanced and nimble and dynamic way”, and put more responsibility on so-called frontier labs who were developing new areas of the technology to make sure it was safe.

“We don’t want to stifle the innovation, all the amazing things that come out of it. We want those things, but also there’s no complete consensus even [among] people working on this – the scientists and the researchers working on this – [about] what exactly the risks are and how big they are,” he said.

He said a framework that could quickly adapt to test critical elements of the systems, keeping up with the technology in a way that regulation would struggle to do, would be needed.

Speaking at the opening of the event, European Commission vice-president with responsibility for tech sovereignty Henna Virkkunen said incidents of hacking and so-called rogue AI undermine trust in the technology.

AI systems should adopt safety lessons from nuclear industry

“The commission has been loud and clear: AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control, and we stand ready to take all necessary steps to ensure companies follow AI Act rules so that European people can trust AI models and innovations.”

Stripe’s Eileen O’Mara said the technology also presented an opportunity for economies.

“What we are seeing is a complete replatform of the economy. AI companies are going global faster than any other cohort of any in [software as a service] land in history. That’s really unique,” she said.

“AI in this economy should be one that brings everybody with it. This is an opportunity for everybody to have an opportunity to drive productivity and growth, and most importantly for Europe to drive meaningful entrepreneurship and drive business.”

The event was opened by Taoiseach Micheál Martin, who said there was a desire for “responsible, safe and secure AI” with AI benefits “guided and guarded by human agency”.

The technology has the potential to improve services, he said, but there was a need to cut through the noise, hype and rhetoric to zero in on the opportunities that could answer many of the challenges facing Europe today.

]]>Bryan Meade<![CDATA[Daktronics to close Clare facility with the loss of over 100 jobs]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/daktronics-to-close-clare-facility-with-the-loss-of-over-100-jobs/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/daktronics-to-close-clare-facility-with-the-loss-of-over-100-jobs/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 18:56:23 +0000US-headquartered electronic display system firm Daktronics is to close its manufacturing facility in Ennistymon in north Clare with the loss of over 100 jobs.

In an announcement on Wednesday, Daktronics said the closure is anticipated to be substantially complete by the middle of 2028.

The move follows Daktronics’s decision to exit the portion of the business which serves rail, bus, and roadway customers outside of North America.

The company said the action was “intended to reduce fixed costs with a low or negative return outlook and improve manufacturing utilisation across the company’s global manufacturing network”.

President and chief executive officer (CEO) of Daktronics, Ramesh Jayaraman, said “exiting Ireland and aligning our manufacturing capacity will help us manage factory utilisation across the network more effectively, improve workforce productivity, set the stage for further automation, and streamline procurement initiatives”.

“We are taking these steps to meet the evolving needs of our customers,” he said.

The company’s vice-president for international markets, Judd Guthmiller said the decision to cease manufacturing operations in Ireland “has been a very difficult decision and has not been taken lightly, but market realities have made it unavoidable”.

“It does not diminish the enormous contribution our Ireland colleagues have made to the company and to our customers and our focus now is on supporting the team through the closure process in the best way possible.”

AI companies should ‘sell solutions’ rather than ‘fear’, conference hears

Wednesday’s announcement followed the company confirming at the start of September that it was entering a collective redundancy consultation after it informed its employees that their positions were at risk.

In its statement, the company said leaving Ireland was expected to result in $13.5 million (€12 million) of cumulative pretax charges, including employee-related costs, facility wind-down and equipment-transfer costs, and also potential asset impairments.

Daktronics said, when fully implemented, the closure was expected to generate $7.7 million of annualised pretax savings which, it said, will fully offset the associated implementation costs in less than two years “while contributing to the company’s broader structural cost reduction and margin improvement objectives”.

The most recent accounts for Daktronics Ireland Co Ltd showed that the company was profitable.

For the 12 months to the end of April 2025, the firm recorded a pretax profit of €586,003 as revenues decreased by 8.5 per cent from €17.98 million to €16.44 million.

The company at the end of April 2025 employed 116 and staff costs for the year totalled €6.49 million.

Tech leaders outline AI dangers and opportunities at Dublin summit

]]>Cheng Xin<![CDATA[AI firms should ‘sell solutions’ rather than ‘fear’, OpenAI executive tells Dublin summit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/ai-companies-should-sell-solutions-rather-than-fear-conference-hears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/ai-companies-should-sell-solutions-rather-than-fear-conference-hears/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 17:45:47 +0000Artificial intelligence (AI) companies should be “selling solutions” in areas such as cybersecurity rather than “selling fear”, OpenAI executive Sarah Friar told a summit in Dublin on Wednesday as the firm targets future growth.

The company may also find more opportunities in areas such as life sciences, drug development and the microchip industry, she said.

Friar, OpenAI’s chief financial officer, was speaking at the International AI Summit at the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin.

The event, organised by the Government as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union, brought together leaders from industry and government across the region to discuss the opportunities and challenges brought by the technology.

The executive told the summit that AI had a role to play in shoring up systems, discovering vulnerabilities in older code and patching them at “machine speed”.

“Selling fear is not a good way to come to the world. We have to sell solutions and solutions that feel transparent, open and honest,” Friar said.

There have been fears that the technology will eliminate many jobs, even in the tech sector.

However, she told The Irish Times the number of software developers had increased globally rather than fallen off.

“If you look at the amount of code that can be developed, it has gone way up,” she said. “So if software has eaten the world, to quote [US businessman] Marc Andreessen, we are now just having that happening at an even faster rate.”

What may change, she said, was how people learned to develop software, and new jobs would be – and were being – created through and because of AI.

The AI company has seen significant growth in Ireland, with more than 2.5 million people here using ChatGPT every week, out of 1.2 billion globally.

OpenAI has yet to turn a profit and has raised more than $180 billion (€161.8 billion) in funding, including $122 billion in the first quarter of the year. Recent reports put overall annualised revenues for the company at $50 billion, around $20 billion below previous reports.

OpenAI began selling ads on its ChatGPT platform this year. It recorded an annualised revenue run rate of $1 billion for the ad business as of the end of August. But Friar said trust in the technology was key.

“You have to have trust with your user and be very clear what are your principles off the bat. We’re very clear that you get the best outcome from the model, not the sponsored outcome,” Friar told The Irish Times.

“I think we are a very interesting ad platform because we’re kind of this beautiful meld of high contextual relevance.”

In a speech at the event, Microsoft president Brad Smith called for stricter safety rules for AI, saying there were more safety rules for ovens and cartons of milk than there were for AI.

“Let’s be devoted to the progress of technology, but let’s be even more devoted to the advance of humanity,” he said.

“Think about your kids. Think about our neighbours and remember this: people are more important than AI.”

He said he was optimistic about what AI could do for Europe, with a new generation of technology that created more important opportunities and responsibilities than before.

]]>Cillian Sherlock<![CDATA[Background costs comprise more than 50% of consumers’ electricity bills]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/work-on-north-south-power-line-to-start-next-year-minister/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/work-on-north-south-power-line-to-start-next-year-minister/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 10:12:56 +0000Network, regulatory, policy and other costs account for more than half of what Irish people pay for electricity, new research shows.

The Republic has the most expensive electricity in the European Union, with households paying 40 cent a kilowatt-hour, almost €1,700 a year, on average, for their power, 40 per cent more than the European average.

Network charges, the cost of incentives to lure investment in new power plants, the impact of policy and regulations, and other expenses now account for 55 per cent of what households pay for electricity, research by a new think tank, Trifecta Ireland, shows.

And the non-electricity costs can make up an even greater share of bills paid by some industries, Trifecta Ireland chief executive Conall Bolger noted at the launch of the organisation’s report titled What Can Move the Needle on Bills before 2030, on Wednesday.

The report proposes 17 measures that could cut electricity costs in the shorter term while investment in power plants and long-term improvements to the national grid and distribution networks are under way.

Bolger noted that the changes focused on aiding electricity customers. “We need to use existing networks more efficiently, we need to make the system more flexible, and we need to get more out of what we have,” he said.

The proposals include mass retrofitting of social housing, reforming the system for paying power plants to remain on standby when they are not generating electricity, more focused supports for families in energy poverty, and various measures to encourage electrification and to give homes and businesses flexibility to use electricity at times when it is cheaper.

Work on a long-delayed cross-Border power line that could cut €150 million a year from electricity bills will begin next year, Minister for Energy Darragh O’Brien pledged at the launch.

Planning and political controversies have delayed construction of the North-South Interconnector, a high-voltage electricity line running from Co Meath to Co Tyrone that was first proposed 20 years ago.

O’Brien said on Wednesday that work should begin on the project next year as it now has full planning permission.

“It’s going to be built,” the Minister emphasised. He told a conference that the power line would be subject to “no more reviews” and noted that four studies had weighed whether it was possible to run the line underground rather than on pylons.

“It will deliver reductions in energy bills of up to €150 million annually,” added O’Brien.

Trifecta’s Ireland research drew on more than 40 State, civil society and energy industry organisations. Funded by the family of Irish renewable energy industry pioneer, Eddie O’Connor, Trifecta Ireland focuses on how to provide an electricity system that is affordable, clean and secure.

]]><![CDATA[Teaching unions urge Taoiseach to intervene and prevent further strike action]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/education/2026/10/14/teaching-unions-urge-taoiseach-to-intervene-and-prevent-further-strike-action/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/education/2026/10/14/teaching-unions-urge-taoiseach-to-intervene-and-prevent-further-strike-action/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 17:52:14 +0000Leaders of the main teaching unions have called for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to intervene in order to prevent further strike action on the first day of industrial action over pay.

Speaking on a picket line outside Hartstown Community College in Dublin 15 on Wednesday, the general secretaries of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation (INTO), the Association of Secondary Teachers in Ireland (ASTI) and the Teachers’ Union of Ireland (TUI) all indicated a lack of trust between their members and the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform.

Almost all schools, colleges and universities countrywide were closed on Wednesday in the biggest public sector strike seen here for almost two decades.

‘Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting’: Live updates

Approximately 100,000 teachers and lecturers who are members of the INTO, ASTI, TUI and the Irish Federation of University Teachers (IFUT) went on strike over what they called a lack of meaningful engagement from Government on a new public sector pay deal.

In total, there were more than 300,000 public sector workers, including teachers, doctors, nurses and civil servants, taking part in Wednesday’s strike.

“I think it’s fairly evident there’s been a breakdown of trust. And I think really we’re going to need somebody to bring the parties together,” said ASTI general secretary Linda Kelly.

“I think it was too little, too late from the Minister [for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers] last night to have his epiphany around pay being a central part of a pay deal. And I think that needs to be addressed. I do think there is a role here for the Taoiseach,” said Kelly.

Chambers told RTÉ’s Prime Time last night that pay could be dealt with first in any negotiations.

“The question is, can we trust that now?” said INTO general secretary John Boyle.

“This is the same Minister who told the general public only three weeks before the budget that there will be €2 billion available for public service pay, and yet on budget day, he only made available €1 billion, plus point two of a billion for pensions. And within the €1 billion, a lot of that money is already spent on carry-over costs.

“So we are going to have to get assurances from the Taoiseach, who needs to step in here, that whatever negotiations are going to commence, and I am confident that they will commence after last night’s change of heart from the Minister, but the Taoiseach is going to have to convince us that if pay is going to be spoken about at the beginning of the talks, that it’s all aspects of pay,” said Boyle.

Meanwhile, TUI general secretary Michael Gillespie said there is a “feeling that the industrial relations machinery of the country is not being taken seriously by one department [of Public Expenditure].

“Unions need to see some sort of wording from both the Department of Public Expenditure and the Cabinet that acknowledges the cost of living crisis and that public sector workers need a pay rise. Then we could go into talks.”

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Microsoft president Brad Smith: Ireland is ‘well-positioned for future of AI’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/podcasts/inside-business/microsoft-president-brad-smith-ireland-is-well-positioned-for-future-of-ai/https://www.irishtimes.com/podcasts/inside-business/microsoft-president-brad-smith-ireland-is-well-positioned-for-future-of-ai/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 15:22:25 +0000This week’s guest on Inside Business is Brad Smith, vice chair and president at tech giant Microsoft.

He was in Dublin this week to speak at the Government’s International AI Summit in the RDS.

Brad sat down with host Ciarán Hancock to discuss the need for regulation of AI, both globally and for individual states, Ireland’s potential role in the development of the technology and how it could change our lives and workplaces.

He also spelled out Microsoft’s own plans and ambitions for AI development in the coming years.

Produced by John Casey with JJ Vernon on sound.

]]><![CDATA[Netflix to cut 1,000 jobs as growth concerns mount]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/netflix-to-cut-1000-jobs-as-growth-concerns-mount/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/netflix-to-cut-1000-jobs-as-growth-concerns-mount/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 16:44:50 +0000Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs, its largest lay-off in four years, as the streaming group grapples with a declining share price and mounting pressure to boost engagement on its platform.

The cuts, equivalent to about 6 per cent of its global staff, will primarily impact employees in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and human resources divisions.

According to an internal memo, Netflix co-chief executives Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters told staff the company needed to be more “disciplined”.

For the 65 per cent of Irish adults who say they have at least one, the launch last week of a new second-hand online marketplace here by the Swedish giant will be good news.

Irish fans of the world’s biggest furniture retailer are legion. Its Ballymun shop was its best performing store globally in 2023, with some 3.2 million customers walking through the door. Total retail sales here reached €247.3 million last year, with Irish customers buying more of Ikea’s moving boxes and red wine glasses than any other country in the world.

Now, you will be able to flog your old Ikea furniture and buy preloved items on the cheap through the retailer too. So how will it work, can you make money, why is Ikea doing it – and during this Climate Action Week, is it really any good for the environment?

New marketplace

The launch of Ikea’s second-hand marketplace means customers who have signed up to the company’s Ikea Family membership scheme can connect to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally. Think eBay, Vinted or Facebook Marketplace – but only for Ikea goods.

The new digital second-hand shop will make it easier for people to make some money from old Ikea furniture they no longer need, while helping others to find discounted, pre-owned items, including those no longer available in stores, says Ikea.

The only things you can’t resell are kitchen accessories, mattresses and food.

The launch here follows successful trials by the Swedish company of online second-hand marketplaces in Spain, Norway, Portugal, Poland, Sweden and Belgium.

In those countries, demand has been strongest for bedroom furniture, storage solutions and livingroom sofas and chairs. The company’s Kallax storage cubes and its Malm chest of drawers have emerged as two of the most popular items being traded second-hand to date.

Items are being listed for less than half of their full retail price, says Ikea.

“When we look at the average reduction in price for items listed, it’s 60 per cent or less,” says Greg Lucas, sustainability manager, Ikea UK and Ireland.

Got your eye on the popular Malm Storklinta chest of six drawers? These had been retailing new this summer for €160; now you could nab a set second-hand and in good nick for just €96.

That Besta TV unit that was retailing for €255? If the retailer’s predictions are correct, you could now secure a preloved model from another Ikea Family member for about €100.

Ikea has already cut its prices on about 1,500 products by between 15 and 25 per cent in 20 European countries, including Ireland, since September 1st. The move was an attempt by the flat-pack furniture retailer to counter the cost-of-living crisis as consumer confidence continues to remain depressed.

So, if you are selling products second-hand that you bought before the price drop, you may not recoup quite so much of your original spend.

Selling and buying

Unlike some second-hand marketplaces, sellers on Ikea’s site can sell for free, at least for now. Selling through some competing third-party sites can attract fees.

For example, a second-hand Ikea Kallax for sale in Ireland on Vinted right now is priced at €25, but a fee of €1.95 is charged to “cover the cost of providing a safe smooth experience for our community”, says Vinted.

Posting a product for sale on the Ikea site is arguably easier too. Sellers simply tick the product they are selling from Ikea’s vast library, and their ad will pre-populate with the exact description and dimensions, with links to spare parts. Some small spare parts are free. Sellers can also post photos of the item they have taken themselves.

“It’s down to the buyer to highlight what condition it’s in today,” says Lucas.

Helpfully, buyers can post reviews of sellers too, which should help to keep community members honest.

You can choose to receive payment by bank transfer or opt for an Ikea digital refund card – which will give sellers a 15 per cent bonus.

Sellers accepting payment via the refund card can use the credit against new Ikea products. You can also use it to buy other second-hand products in store through the company’s Buyback and Resell service.

The pleasures of Vinted have often little to do with money, although the cash is nice

This service enables customers to sell eligible products back to Ikea in exchange for in-store credit. By enabling this, Ikea may be countering criticism that the 15 per cent bonus incentivises us back into the shop to buy yet more new stuff on a planet on which there is already too much stuff.

You can also use the card to buy food at Ikea.

When an item is purchased, payment is held securely by Ikea’s payment service provider until the buyer has collected or received the item and confirms acceptance through the marketplace. At that point, a 48-hour buyer protection period begins.

During this period, the buyer can raise an issue if the product does not match its listing. For example, buyers can contact support if there are missing parts, undisclosed damage, or if the item is not an authentic Ikea product.

If there are no issues, payment is automatically released to the seller.

If there is an issue, the payment remains on hold while a refund request is reviewed in line with the marketplace’s buyer protection policy. Ikea says it can support dispute resolution where needed.

While there are no fees on the Irish site for now, the company has introduced a “buyer protection fee” in Spain, which it says supports “safeguards”, like ensuring only authentic Ikea products in usable condition are advertised and only by Ikea Family members.

Delivery

Sellers and buyers will have to arrange delivery and/or pickup between themselves. But with Ikea products so ubiquitous in Irish homes, you probably won’t have a hard time finding a Billy bookcase or Kallax cube near you.

Indeed, after just 10 years in the State, some 65 per cent of Irish adults say they have at least one Ikea product in their home, according to research the company published in July 2019 to mark that 10th anniversary.

One in four people in Ireland surveyed said that Ikea was their go-to when moving into a new home, with another 21 per cent saying they visited the furniture giant when planning their first home with their partner. Some 70 per cent of Irish parents said they had Ikea products in their home.

Despite the lack of a delivery service, buying second-hand could prove more convenient than buying new. Finding a good-as-new Poang chair for sale in your own town will spare you the schlep to Ballymun, where a tour of the gargantuan shop has been known to test the most solid of relationships.

What Irish shoppers love to buy in Ikea

Ikea says it is “exploring” a “convenient, affordable and sustainable” delivery service for bulky items, says Lucas.

It piloted the use of TipTapp in Sweden and Lisbon this summer. This is a peer-to-peer mobile app that matches people who need help moving or delivering items with people who have a car and spare time.

“Once the Ikea online marketplace purchase is completed, the buyer can post a ‘delivery task’, set the price they are prepared to pay for delivery and receive offers from available ‘helpers’,” says Ikea.

They can compare helper ratings and reviews, choose a helper, track delivery in real time and pay securely once the item arrives. For those who just can’t wait for that Poang chair, collection and delivery may even be available on the same day.

Ikea’s timing in Ireland is something to behold. Maybe it’s not so much the Scandi-inspired aesthetic that resonates with us so much as its ability to meet the moment. And we’ve had our moments.

Ikea opened its big blue Lego-like superstore in Dublin 11 in 2009 at the height of Ireland’s financial crash. Yes, its furniture was mass-produced and everywhere, but it was also affordable at a time when roughly 150,000 mortgage borrowers had plunged into negative equity, according to estimates from the Economic and Social Research Institute think tank, with house prices dropping from their early-2007 peak.

The higher-end furniture retailer Habitat had shut up shop in Dublin and Galway in 2008 due, it said, to a “severe” deterioration in sales.

‘Vinted is a wolf in sheep’s clothing’: Ireland’s vintage stores on facing down online challenges

Now, almost 20 years on from the crash, we find ourselves punch-drunk from another cost-of-living crisis and an ongoing housing crisis, and with further economic clouds scrambling on the horizon. The launch of Ikea’s second-hand selling website here on the day Budget 2027 was unveiled is well timed, or portentous.

Being able to furnish your entire home and garden affordably and from one retailer, using new or second-hand products, is not to be sniffed at. Even if everyone in your estate has the same Billy bookcase.

Slice of the pie

Second-hand shopping has become big business, and Ikea knows it. It has emerged as a “quiet but significant shift” in Irish consumer behaviour, according to analysis by RedC.

It’s no longer a niche trend confined to charity shops, vintage enthusiasts or bargain hunters. Increasingly, it is becoming a normal part of everyday consumer behaviour in Ireland, says RedC.

It’s not just a way to save money but part of a broader move towards more sustainable and circular patterns of consumption. Second-hand shopping is becoming an established part of life here.

Brands are having to rethink how they compete in a world where new products increasingly sit alongside refurbished, reused and preloved alternatives.

More than nine in 10 adults in Ireland say they shop for second-hand goods, according to research commissioned by Ikea in September. Some 45 per cent of adults said they buy pre-owned furniture.

Are you a fool to pay full price? From paint to phones, buying second-hand can slash your costs

No doubt Ikea has been watching established second-hand marketplaces like eBay, Facebook Marketplace and Vinted steal its Swedish meatball lunch. Those platforms are full of listings of second-hand Ikea items, likely hitting sales of new Ikea products while returning nothing to the retailer.

So now, Ikea is getting in on the act. By launching its own second-hand marketplace here, it is harvesting something back from this thriving second-hand market of its own products. By incentivising payment through an Ikea digital refund card, money from transacting its products second-hand gets directed back to Ikea.

But is it green?

Buying second hand is great, says the Rediscovery Centre, the National Centre for the Circular Economy, but buying less overall, and repairing what you have, is better.

“The bigger challenge is that, in Ireland, we simply consume too much,” says Claire Downey, chief executive of the Rediscovery Centre, which is headquartered just over a kilometre from Ikea’s Ballymun outlet.

Irish homes contain an average of €531 worth of unused home and garden furniture, according to Ikea’s research, and unused home decor and accessories worth an average of €347. Yikes.

That baby changing table you bought new, and used only for a few short years, could have been borrowed.

“Many of the things we buy are not needed for long. Borrowing, sharing and renting are great alternatives to buying and they help to reduce the amount of stuff we accumulate in the first place, as well as saving money and space in our homes,” says Downey.

Ikea’s tantalising promise is that we are all just one good shoe rack away from nirvana

Circular.ie and Repairmystuff.ie are digital platforms that support communities to reduce consumption and waste by sharing, reusing and repairing, she says.

Many of the things we spend money replacing could easily be repaired, says Downey.

“We’d love to see a shift in mindset where people automatically consider repairing, renting and borrowing, or buying second-hand before buying new.”

Before you go thinking the housing crisis has been solved, hold on. What we are seeing is not evidence of that. Prices nationally remain 44 per cent above pre-Covid levels. The easing we’re seeing is not driven by new supply. It reflects two developments: first, buyers are reaching the limit of what income, lending rules and support schemes allow them to pay, and second, the homes that are being built don’t match what people want.

We are still building three-bed semidetached homes in commuter towns, in a country that wants urban apartments, because the size and nature of the Irish household has changed. We are having fewer children, and more people are single and want to live alone or in a couple without necessarily wanting two extra bedrooms.

Let’s look at the first development. Prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit the price ceiling. The expression “the cure for high prices is high prices” is one of the oldest in economics. Eventually, very high prices fix themselves by depressing demand, because people run out of money and can’t afford to pay the higher prices. In addition, the high prices usually imply higher profits for builders and the higher prices prompt higher supply, which brings down prices in time. However, in Ireland right now, it is a simple fact that buyers are “maxed out” and can’t afford relentless rises in house prices – so they cannot play the game any longer.

Since Covid, although wages have been more or less rising in line with inflation or a small bit more, house prices across the country are up massively. In Munster, outside the cities, prices are up 72 per cent since the pandemic. They are up 62 per cent in Leinster outside Dublin; the four regional cities have seen prices rise by 57 per cent, while in Connaught/Ulster, traditionally the most moribund of housing markets, prices are up a whopping 72 per cent since Covid.

If Irish property is overvalued, will house prices fall?

Dublin lags behind, with prices up by 32 per cent in the same period. The current asking price for a three-bed semi is €635,000 in Dublin, €431,000 in Cork city, €424,000 in Galway city; €376,000 in Limerick City and €313,000 in Waterford city.

The font of all borrowing is income, so let’s look at these prices relative to wages and the ability to borrow, and then let’s see where prices should be. Real wages are roughly flat: earnings were up 3.9 per cent against inflation of 3.7 per cent last year. First-time buyers – half of all buyers – can borrow, at most, four times their income, with a 10 per cent deposit.

This is a numbers game – and the numbers don’t add up. We need far more apartments in our cities, and the asking prices for these apartments must fall

So take a couple in their 30s, both on average earnings of €1,046.88 a week, or €54,400 a year. This gives them €108,900 combined. Four times income in borrowings means a maximum mortgage of €435,500. When adding their 10 per cent deposit, the maximum purchase price they can afford is about €484,000.

Based on these figures, the Dublin family home is out of reach on their income alone. The couple would need a dual income of about €145,000 to afford the three-bed semi, or a cool €200,000 in cash.

In terms of getting an apartment in Dublin, the average two-bed costs €406,000, so it is within lending limits, and repayments are below 20 per cent of gross income. The challenge for this couple is saving up the €41,000 in cash for a deposit, roughly 4.5 months of combined gross pay.

This is not insurmountable if they have been saving, or can rely on family, and parents giving a house deposit to young couples is very common. But let’s say they would like to have a family in an urban setting, in, say, a three-bed apartment. At a cost of €502,000 it is about €18,000 over the couple’s maximum threshold, and it would require €66,500 in cash.

The Irish Times view on the ESRI housing report: house prices alarmingly overvalued

Even if taking the completely stretched first-time buying couple who’ve looked down the back of the couch to put together every cent they have, they are still well short of the needed funds in Dublin. Is it any surprise prices are adjusting in the capital?

Apologies for all the numbers in the last few paragraphs, but this is a numbers game – and the numbers don’t add up. We need far more apartments in our cities, and the asking prices for these apartments must fall. The State must fast-track building in the cities. We need to build up, because obviously the more floors in a building, the cheaper the apartments ultimately built will be – and we also need to reduce the ability of serial objectors to put spurious spanners in the works.

For now, the market has spoken – prices are adjusting downwards, because the cure for high prices is high prices.

Long may this last.

None of this is good for O’Donovan’s political reputation, and there were mutterings from various unnamed Government figures over the weekend that he might not keep his Cabinet seat when the midterm reshuffle takes place at the end of next year.

The Limerick TD seems to have an unfortunate knack for losing friends and alienating people, but last week’s embarrassments and the subsequent clean-up may have forced the question of how RTÉ is funded back on to the agenda, and that would not be a bad thing.

The current arrangement was agreed by the previous government in the summer of 2024. It guaranteed RTÉ €725 million in public money over three years, rising from €225 million in 2025 to €240 million this year and €260 million in 2027. The licence fee was retained, and the Exchequer committed to making up the difference between what it brought in and the agreed total. The lower amount raised from licence revenue, the bigger the cheque from the State.

That difference is growing quickly. Licence sales have fallen every year since the 2023 payments scandal. Free licences grow by up to 20,000 a year as the population ages, while paid ones keep falling. Remarkably, if current trends hold, licences paid for by social protection will outnumber those paid for by households as early as 2029. This seems untenable.

Does Patrick O’Donovan’s explanation for €20m RTÉ funding cut add up?

Add the direct top-up and the picture is starker still. In 2025, about 54 per cent of RTÉ’s public funding came from the Exchequer in one form or another. By 2027, that share is likely to be above 60 per cent. The licence fee survives in name, but the money increasingly comes directly from Government.

European law now has something to say about this. The European Media Freedom Act requires member states to fund public broadcasters through transparent procedures based on objective criteria set in advance, and to ensure they have “adequate, sustainable and predictable” resources. The point is to protect editorial independence by making sure money cannot be used as a political lever. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill now before the Oireachtas is meant to give effect to those rules here.

Last week’s episode looks much more like political incompetence than a deliberate act of interference. But cutting an agreed sum at a few hours’ notice, without explanation, is clearly not in keeping with the spirit of the EU rules. Whatever its cause, it has shown how easily the money can be turned on and off.

Nor should the role of ill-will be underestimated. Members of the Oireachtas media committee have indicated they intend to question RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst about a newspaper column by radio presenter Oliver Callan, which questioned Simon Harris’s credentials as Minister for Finance. That the two are being raised alongside each other is telling.

The new legislation will strengthen the role of Coimisiún na Meán, which will assess RTÉ’s needs and recommend a level of funding for each three-year period. But the regulator’s role will be advisory. There will be no legal obligation on the minister of the day to follow its recommendations, nor, as far as can be seen, any requirement to explain a decision not to. The final call will remain where it was last week, with a politician putting together a budget.

The licence fee has many faults, including the fact that it is now collapsing before our eyes. But it was based on a sound principle. Money paid directly by citizens to a public service broadcaster, at arm’s length from the government of the day, gave that broadcaster a degree of independence that an annual grant cannot.

If public service broadcasting is to retain public trust and integrity, it must be insulated from political pressure, whether born of malice or just haplessness. If nothing else, we can thank O’Donovan for reminding us of that.

The net cost to you is determined by two things: fee per band and the personal subsidy to which each child is entitled, depending on your income.

Under the budget measures, the fee for Band F will fall from €336 a week to €300. And, for those on the universal subsidy (anyone with family income of more than €73,000), the subsidy for children up to senior infants will rise to €2.50 from €2.15 per hour up to a maximum of 45 hours.

If your income is below €73,000, the subsidy may be higher and, if it is below €36,500, that could be as high as €5.10 an hour.

When they say household income, they mean income minus any pension contributions you pay. You also do not include certain welfare payments and, if you have more than one child, there are further income disregards.

Anyway, back to the numbers. That €2.50 an hour universal subsidy amounts to €112.50 a week. Taking this from your €300 “fee”, you are left with €187.50. From September next year (11 months in the future), that will be your weekly fee, amounting to €750 a month.

That means a fall of at least €209 in your childcare cost per child each month, or somewhere between €2,300 and €2,500 over the year. So good news, if not quite a drop in charge to €550.

Of course, that is only if you are in a creche that operates under Government core funding. If not, they are free to charge what the market will bear.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445058/">
   <title>KI-Gipfel spaltet EU-Tech-Hauptstadt Dublin</title>
   <description>Tech-Bosse und -Persönlichkeiten von OpenAI bis Microsoft sind am Mittwoch in Dublin mit hochrangigen Vertreterinnen und Vertreten aus Europas Politik zusammengetroffen. Die irische Hauptstadt unterstrich mit dem großen Gipfel zum Thema künstliche Intelligenz (KI) ihre Rolle als wichtiges Bindeglied zwischen Big Tech und Europa. Die Zivilgesellschaft war praktisch nicht auf der Veranstaltung vertreten – sie protestierte unterdessen vor der Tür gegen die US-Konzerne. Aber auch gleichzeitig stattfindende Proteste des öffentlichen Dienstes zeigen, dass neben KI auch andere Themen Irland spalten.</description>

In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK

— Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did.

"I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.

However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).

The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples

It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026

In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”.

Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”.

]]> Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/14/norwegian-defence-firm-kongsberg-to-build-anti-drone-factory-in-poland/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 10:10:08 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105500

Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs.

“The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation.

In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year.

Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8

— Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks.

While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast.

Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028.

 

Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.

Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia.

The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus.

Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe.

The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026

Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.

In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.

Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology.

On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

]]> New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/14/new-polish-constitutional-court-judge-takes-oath-in-defiance-of-president/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 08:52:44 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105505

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M

— Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

1294/2026

Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo

— Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026

Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him.

However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government).

Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS.

In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions.

Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026

Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal.

Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog.

So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK.

Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026

Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry.

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”.

This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

Nawrocki also plans to visit G20 members Saudi Arabia and Argentina to canvass for support for Poland’s membership bid, Przydacz has confirmed.

A third option would be for Poland to become a “permanent guest”, a status typically reserved for organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, but also held by Spain.

Last December, the US invited Poland to join this year’s summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Poland was “assuming its rightful place” at the forum.

Poland has argued that its membership is justified by its economy being on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world.

Though G20 membership is not decided solely on that basis, the G20 does include most of the world’s 20 largest economies (only Switzerland and the Netherlands have larger economies than Poland but no G20 membership).

Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. Turnout was 44.3%.

“Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.”

Gibała’s victory had been expected after he came top in the first round two weeks ago with 36.4% of the vote among the seven candidates who stood. Piątkowska trailed on 29.9%. The top two candidates then met in today’s run-off.

 

Piątkowska was the joint candidate of Tusk’s centrist KO party and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which are both part of the national government.

Among her campaign promises were to seek to locate an AI “gigafactory” in Kraków, to boost the availability of housing for young people, and to implement a package of policies for women, including free mammograms, pram-friendly infrastructure, free menstrual hygiene products, and safer nighttime public transport.

A petition to hold a recall referendum received more than the 58,355 signatures required. Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”.

The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party).

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.

They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury

Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków…

— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 14 Oct 2026 17:40:08 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 London listings fall to lowest levels since 2023 https://www.cityam.com/london-listings-fall-to-lowest-levels-since-2023/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 23:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465689
